I wrote `/tmp/obench-cell-wleioj7f/bench_opencode_polyglot-rust-c_9qpzycdy/polyglot/main.rs`. Both `rustc` and `g++ -x c++` compile it. I ran both binaries for N = 0, 1, 2, 10 and 100. They printed the same values each time: 1, 1, 2, 89 and 573147844013817084101.

One caveat: I compiled with `rustc ... -o polyglot/main`. Your command has no `-o`, so `rustc` will write the `main` binary to your current directory. That means `/tmp/.../polyglot/main N` only works if you run it from inside `polyglot/`.

It works by hiding each language's code from the other compiler:
- **Opening trick:** The first line is `//\`. C++ treats the backslash as a line continuation, so the next line (`/*`) becomes part of the comment. Rust sees a one-line comment, then a real `/*` that opens a block comment.
- **C++ code:** It sits inside that Rust block comment, followed by `#if 0`.
- **Closing trick:** The line `//*/ */ */` is a plain line comment to C++. To Rust, it opens one nested comment and closes two, which ends the outer comment. This is needed because Rust block comments nest and C++ ones don't.
- **Rust code:** It sits inside the C++ `#if 0` block. A second `//\` / `/*` / `#endif` / `//*/ */ */` sequence at the end closes the `#if 0` for C++ and hides the `#endif` from Rust.

Both versions use 128-bit integers, so they are correct up to about N = 185. Past that, Rust panics on overflow, while C++ wraps around silently.
